meta.title: MCP Question Bank — Chapter 17: AAIF & Agentic Ecosystem
meta.revision: v2.1 (curated 2026-09-12, 200 items, verified against the 2026-07-28 specification)

questions.question: Which projects anchored the Agentic AI Foundation at its December 2025 launch, and who contributed them?

options.text: MCP and goose from Anthropic, AGENTS.md from the Linux Foundation
MCP from Anthropic, goose from Block, AGENTS.md from OpenAI
MCP from Anthropic, LangChain from LangChain Inc, AGENTS.md from GitHub
MCP from Anthropic, agentgateway from Solo.io, AGENTS.md from OpenAI

questions.explanation: The AAIF launched on 9 December 2025 anchored by MCP (Anthropic), goose (Block) and AGENTS.md (OpenAI). agentgateway, from Solo.io, joined later, in June 2026.

questions.question: A teammate adds an AGENTS.md file to your repository and asks you to keep it current. What role does that file play?

options.text: An authorization config that scopes what an agent may do in a given repository
A markdown convention that hands coding agents project-specific instructions
A registry file listing the agents allowed to open pull requests
A changelog format that records which agents modified a repository

questions.explanation: AGENTS.md is a convention for giving AI coding agents consistent, project-specific guidance, released by OpenAI in August 2025 and contributed to the AAIF at launch, with adoption across tens of thousands of projects. It is not a changelog, a registry or an auth config.

questions.question: Which practical benefit does the ecosystem get from MCP being a shared standard rather than a vendor API?

options.text: A server written once works with any MCP client, with no vendor lock-in
Servers can assume all clients implement sampling and roots
Every host is guaranteed to support the same set of extensions and primitives
Hosts can execute a server's tools without asking the user

questions.explanation: Portability is the point: write the server once and any compliant client can use it. Extension support varies by client, sampling and roots are deprecated and were always optional, and consent requirements do not go away.

questions.question: Your architecture board asks what MCP's move under a foundation changes for a company betting on it. What is the substantive answer?

options.text: Governance is neutral and open, so no single vendor can unilaterally change or withdraw it
The foundation hosts the registry's servers, so availability is underwritten
The foundation indemnifies adopters against any licensing claim brought over the specification
The foundation certifies conforming servers, so compatibility is guaranteed

questions.explanation: Foundation stewardship is about neutral, open governance under known licences and a public process, which is the risk an adopter cares about. There is no conformance certification, no hosting guarantee and no indemnity.

questions.question: A teammate proposes replacing your MCP server with an AGENTS.md file. Why do the two not substitute for each other?

options.text: AGENTS.md is a registry manifest; MCP is the protocol that reads that manifest at runtime
AGENTS.md is the legacy format that MCP's prompts primitive replaced in 2026-07-28
AGENTS.md gives an agent static repository instructions; MCP gives it live context and tools
AGENTS.md configures the host's model choice; MCP configures which servers it connects to

questions.explanation: AGENTS.md is a markdown convention telling coding agents how to work in a repository. MCP is a wire protocol for reaching data and actions at runtime. Both are AAIF projects, and they solve adjacent rather than overlapping problems.

questions.question: Your data team already has a Python library that queries the warehouse. What does wrapping it in an MCP server actually buy?

options.text: The warehouse's access control is replaced by MCP's own permission model
The model can execute the library's code directly inside the host process
Query results are automatically cached and shared between all connected hosts
Every MCP host can use it without bespoke integration code on each side

questions.explanation: The value is the many-to-many problem: one server speaks a standard protocol that any host already knows, so each new application costs nothing extra. MCP does not execute your library in the host, cache across hosts, or replace your backend's authorization.

questions.question: Why does a gateway such as agentgateway benefit specifically from the 2026-07-28 header requirements?

options.text: The headers carry the OAuth token, so the gateway can authorize without reading the body
MCP-Protocol-Version lets it rewrite requests into whichever version the server prefers
Mcp-Session-Id lets it pin each client to one backend replica
Mcp-Method and Mcp-Name let it route, meter and authorize without parsing the JSON body

questions.explanation: Mirroring the method and target into headers is exactly what lets intermediaries apply per-tool rate limits, WAF policy and routing cheaply. Sessions were removed, gateways do not rewrite versions, and the token stays in the Authorization header, which is not new.

questions.question: A support desk wants the assistant to read tickets, draft a reply, and offer a one-click triage workflow. Which mapping fits MCP's primitives?

options.text: All three as tools, since anything reached over the network is a tool call
Tickets as prompts, sending the reply as a tool, the workflow as a resource
Tickets as resources, sending the reply as a tool, the workflow as a prompt
Tickets as tools, sending the reply as a resource, the workflow as a prompt

questions.explanation: Read-only context the application attaches is a resource; an action with effects the model invokes is a tool; a user-chosen workflow template is a prompt. The split follows who controls the primitive, not whether a network call is involved.
